solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cast touring Jersey, say, looking displeased

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the word for cast goes all the way around the animal

parts.note: to cast is to throw, or sling
a Jersey is a breed of dairy cow, the 'say' marking it as an example

explanation.surface: Actors on tour in the Channel Islands look fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a theatre company and 'Jersey' like the island; one is a verb for throwing, the other a breed of cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Scowling is frowning in anger, the face of someone looking displeased.

clue.text: Satisfy head of corporation as soon as French wine's imported

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the word corporation
imported means brought in, so the French word for wine goes inside

parts.note: once can mean as soon as, as in once you arrive
vin is French for wine

explanation.surface: Please the company boss the moment Bordeaux is shipped in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as soon as' is a definition-like phrase here used as a piece: once you arrive means as soon as you arrive. 'imported' is the container signal and 'head of' takes one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To convince someone is to persuade them fully, to satisfy them of a fact.

clue.text: Gradually become less persuasive dancing in the raw

indicators.note: dancing means jiggling about, so the letters of the following words are shuffled

explanation.surface: Losing conviction while capering naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges IN THE RAW.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse or argument that wears thin loses its force through overuse.

clue.text: News two thirds of Ulster's picked up

indicators.note: picked up means lifted, which in a down entry turns the letters upwards

parts.note: six of Ulster's nine counties make up Northern Ireland, NI, so two thirds of Ulster's is of NI

explanation.surface: Reports about most of Northern Ireland have been noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern Ireland, NI, holds six of the nine counties of the old province of Ulster, hence two thirds; 'picked up' turns OF NI upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Info is the casual short form of information, which is news.

clue.text: Measures neck, leg and top of shoulder

parts.note: neck is cheek or nerve, also called gall
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

indicators.note: top of means the first letter of the word, the topmost in a down entry

explanation.surface: A tailor takes measurements of collar, leg and shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neck' means cheek, as in 'what a neck!', not the body part; in cricket, leg and on both name one side of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallons are units of liquid volume, so they are measures.

clue.text: Feel unfit to take charge of coastal vantage point

parts.note: to be achy is to feel sore and out of sorts
to head something is to lead it

explanation.surface: Feeling poorly yet still leading a lookout post by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Beachy Head is a tall chalk headland on the Sussex coast in England; the first word splits as BE ACHY.
explanation.definitionFit: This English cliff top is a famous high headland overlooking the Channel, a lookout spot on the coast.

clue.text: Merry monarch entertaining friends abroad in nightwear

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting, so the king holds the foreign friends inside

parts.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme was a merry old soul
amis is French for friends

explanation.surface: A jolly king has foreign pals round, all in pyjamas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merry monarch' suggests Charles II, but here it is the rhyme's Old King Cole.
explanation.definitionFit: A camisole is a light sleeveless top, often worn as lingerie or for sleeping.

clue.text: Undesirable housing principle blocked by workers

indicators.note: blocked by means obstructed, so the workers sit in the middle of the principle

parts.note: a tenet is a principle or belief
men is a common crossword word for workers

explanation.surface: A rule on homes is stopped by labourers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a run-down block of rented flats, often seen as poor housing.

clue.text: Satisfactory to correspond with Bill

parts.note: a bill posted up is an advertisement, AD for short
to equate things is to make them correspond

explanation.surface: Something matches up well enough with an invoice.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: adequate means good enough, satisfactory.

clue.text: Illicit global union left a load of rubbish

parts.note: the UN, the United Nations, is a worldwide union of states
something awful is dreadful, a load of rubbish

explanation.surface: A worldwide organisation dumps a pile of garbage illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit and unlawful are both synonyms for against the law.

clue.text: Confine false allies holding company back

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the scrambled letters wrap around the reversed abbreviation
false suggests the word allies is not in its true form and must be rearranged
back tells us the abbreviation for company is turned round

explanation.surface: Restrict treacherous partners who are keeping a business under wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' is the anagram signal, 'back' the reversal signal and 'holding' the container signal; the reversed abbreviation lands after the first L of the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To localise something is to restrict it to one area, which is to confine it.

clue.text: Within them, one Yorkshireman keeps rolling

indicators.note: keeps means holds within, so the answer is held inside the run of words before it

explanation.surface: A man from Yorkshire, among a group, carries on tumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across WithIN THEM, ONE Y-orkshireman; 'rolling' is the definition in its slang sense, not motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolling in it is slang for very rich, and being in the money means having plenty of cash.

clue.text: Source of strain when wound up?

definitions.text: Source of strain when wound up?

parts.words: Source of strain when wound up?
parts.note: a strain is a tune, and winding the spring of this small box makes it play

explanation.walkthrough: 'strain' and 'wound up' suggest stress and anger; read musically, they mean a melody and a turned key.
explanation.definitionFit: A clockwork case that plays a tune once its spring has been turned with a key.

clue.text: Fuel for heating drink

definitions.meaning: a solid fuel made by baking coal, burnt in stoves and furnaces
short for Coca-Cola, the fizzy soft drink

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a smokeless solid fuel and, informally, the well-known cola drink.

clue.text: The writer with a home as close as possible

parts.note: in crosswords the writer refers to the setter, giving ME
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: A author with a house that is nearly next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close' here means stingy, not near, which is why 'as close as possible' is a superlative of tight-fistedness.
explanation.definitionFit: Close can mean tight-fisted, so the most close person is the stingiest of all.

clue.text: Eastern trio facing gaol, admitting one's a trickster

parts.note: the Magi were the three wise men from the East

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the gaol takes in the figure one

parts.note: can is slang for prison, gaol
one gives I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Three wise men by a prison, one confessing to being a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: A magician performs illusions, a trickster who deceives audiences for entertainment.

clue.text: Prompt report of busy boat crew

indicators.note: report means something spoken, so we want what the phrase sounds like

parts.note: busy is active, and a rowing crew of eight is an eight

explanation.surface: A rapid account of a hard-working rowing team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' is the verb to trigger, not the adjective for quick.
explanation.definitionFit: To prompt something is to set it going, to trigger or start it off.

clue.text: Polish put up with intrusive female in pursuit of power

indicators.note: in pursuit of means following, so the abbreviation for power comes first and the rest chases it

parts.note: P is the physics abbreviation for power

indicators.note: intrusive means pushing in, so the letter for female forces its way into the word for put up

parts.note: to put up a building is to erect it

explanation.surface: Tolerating a meddling woman who is chasing authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is the verb to refine, not the nationality, despite its capital at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish something is to refine it until flawless, which is to perfect it.

clue.text: Provide ventilation for shelters and leave Spanish Steps

indicators.note: shelters means protects within, so the cooling word wraps round the little word and

parts.note: to fan something is to blow air on it
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Fan the huts and depart via the famous Roman stairway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spanish Steps' looks like the Rome landmark; it is dance steps from Spain. 'shelters' is the container signal, and 'and' is fodder, not a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The fandango is a lively Spanish courtship dance, so its moves are Spanish steps.

clue.text: Top-class youngster makes quick progress

parts.note: crack means first-rate, as in crack troops
a son is a young male child

explanation.surface: An elite child advances rapidly.
explanation.definitionFit: To crack on is a British idiom for pressing ahead briskly with a task.

clue.text: Small, more supple snake

parts.note: lithe means supple, so lither is more supple

explanation.surface: A little, bendier serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snake' is the verb to wriggle along, not the reptile.
explanation.definitionFit: To snake is to move in winding curves, which is to glide or wriggle across the ground.

clue.text: All those attending walk on air

indicators.note: on air means broadcast, spoken over the radio, so we want a word that sounds like another

parts.note: a gait is a manner of walking

explanation.surface: Everyone present is walking on air with delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'walk on air' looks like the idiom for elation; split it, 'walk' gives a word heard and 'on air' says it is heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A gate is the total number of spectators at a sporting event, everyone who attends.

clue.text: Scots, short of a pound appealed to Jock's compatriot

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the letter for a pound is dropped from the phrase

parts.note: if you appealed to someone, you called on them
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
Jock is a stock name for a Scotsman, and Ian is another typical Scottish name

explanation.surface: Scottish people, a quid short, begged a fellow countryman for help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short of' removes one L from CALLED ON, giving CALEDON.
explanation.definitionFit: Caledonia is the old Latin name for Scotland, so its adjective means Scottish.

clue.text: Last two bits of pickle in clandestine spread

indicators.note: in places the picked letters inside the word for clandestine

parts.note: covert means secret, clandestine

indicators.note: last two bits means the final pair of letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Somebody sneaks the final scraps of chutney onto a secret sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' is a bedspread here, not something for bread; 'Last two bits of' picks a pair of letters and 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A coverlet is a bedspread, a light cover laid over a bed.

clue.text: Bottomless side dish, sweet or savoury

indicators.note: bottomless means losing its base, the last letter in a down entry

parts.note: a flank is a side, as of an army or animal

explanation.surface: An endless side order that can be dessert or main.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottomless' drops the final K from FLANK.
explanation.definitionFit: A flan is an open pastry tart that can hold a sweet custard or a savoury filling.

clue.text: Policies adopted by army with no time for purity

indicators.note: adopted by means taken in, so the policies word sits inside the shortened army word
with no tells us a letter is removed from the word for army

parts.note: a host is a large army or multitude
a party's lines are its policies, as in the party line

explanation.surface: A military with no spare time takes up policies of virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' drops T from HOST, leaving HOS, which holds LINES.
explanation.definitionFit: Holiness is the state of being sacred, morally pure and saintly.

clue.text: Rebel church leader disliking work among vacuous people

parts.note: anti means opposed to, disliking

indicators.note: among puts the work abbreviation in the middle of the emptied word
vacuous means empty, so the word people loses its insides, keeping just its outer letters

parts.note: OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A dissident cleric who hates labouring among empty-headed folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacuous' empties a word to its outer letters and 'among' is the container signal; an antipope is a rival pope, so 'Rebel church leader' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An antipope is a rival claimant set up against the legitimately elected Bishop of Rome.

clue.text: Reviews chalky uplands at end of trip

indicators.note: at end of places the uplands word after the word for trip

parts.note: a run is a short trip, as in a run to the shops
the Downs are the rolling chalk hills of southern England

explanation.surface: Assessments of a walk ending on the chalk hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The Downs are the chalk hills of southern England, such as the South Downs.
explanation.definitionFit: A rundown is a summary or review of the main points.
